message:
"Securus" is Latin for (of course) "secure" or "safe." But most people who hear the Latin word today hear it in the context of the Catholic hymn *[Dies Irae](http://www.answers.com/topic/dies-irae)*, or in the symphonic *Requiem* masses of Berlioz, Verdi, and Mozart. "Securus" is the final word in the seventh stanza:

> *Quid sum miser tunc dicturus?
> Quem patronum rogaturus,
> cum vix justus sit securus?*

> What am I, a wretch, to say?
> Upon what advocate can I call,
> When even the just will scarcely be safe?

As [this page](http://www.everything2.com/index.pl?node_id=1485980) points out, "*Cum vix Justus sit securus* reminds us that even the best among us have committed sin" -- a point [Rick Cree](http://www.higcapital.com/09102004.html) seems to entirely have missed. It seems unfortunately un-Christian of Mr. Cree, particularly given his [degree from Southern Methodist University](http://www.t-netix.com/ir/bio/) -- but perhaps Mr. Cree, if he does in fact go to church, subscribes to a faith that privileges profit above all else, and ignores Christ's commandment to "love your neighbor as yourself."
